title: Arabic grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday fluency, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is Modern Standard Arabic, fully vowelled, with a reading in Latin letters.

units.title: Numbers, time and more than one

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first Arabic conversation.
lessons.topic: Sentences without “am, is, are”; {{أَنَا}} “I” and {{أَنْتَ}} / {{أَنْتِ}} “you”

goal.t: مَرْحَبًا، أَنَا سَارَةُ. أَنَا مِنْ كَنَدَا.
goal.r: marḥaban, anā sāratu. anā min kanadā.
goal.tr: Hello, I'm Sarah. I'm from Canada.

blocks.p: Look at what is missing in this conversation: Arabic has no word for “am”, “is” or “are” in the present. {{أَنَا سَارَةُ}} is, word for word, “I Sarah”. You simply put the two side by side.

blocks.means: a group of words that says something complete: I'm from Egypt.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she.

blocks.p: **I and you.** {{أَنَا|anā}} is “I”, for a man or a woman. “You” depends on who you're talking to: {{أَنْتَ|anta}} to a man, {{أَنْتِ|anti}} to a woman. Karim says {{مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتِ؟}} to Sarah, and she answers {{وَأَنْتَ؟}} “and you?”.

**Asking.** The question word comes first: {{مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتَ؟|min ayna anta?}} “Where are you from?”, word for word “from where you?”. And {{وَأَنْتِ؟|wa-anti?}} “and you?” turns any question back to the other person.

ex.note: said by a woman: the ending {{ة}} makes words feminine (a later lesson)
a question just by raising your voice

blocks.tip: The small marks above and below the letters are the vowels (a, i, u): the next lesson shows how to read them. Until then, the reading in Latin letters tells you how to say each example, and tapping an example lets you hear it.

mistakes.why: There is no “am” in the present: put {{أَنَا}} and the word side by side.
Sarah is a woman, so “you” is {{أَنْتِ}}, anti.

practice.q: You're talking to a woman. “You” is…
practice.why: {{أَنْتِ}}, anti, is for a woman; {{أَنْتَ}}, anta, for a man.

practice.q: You're Sami, from Jordan. Choose your replies.

lines.why: About yourself: {{أَنَا}}. (Jordan is “the Jordan” in Arabic: {{الْأُرْدُنُّ}}.)

practice.q: Ask a man: “Where are you from?”
Your turn: say hello, your name and where you're from. Start with {{مَرْحَبًا، أَنَا…}}

answers.t: مَرْحَبًا، أَنَا جُون. أَنَا مِنْ أَمْرِيكَا.
answers.r: marḥaban, anā jūn. anā min amrīkā.
answers.tr: Hello, I'm John. I'm from America.

answers.t: أَهْلًا، أَنَا مَارِيَا. أَنَا مِنْ إِسْبَانِيَا.
answers.r: ahlan, anā māriyā. anā min isbāniyā.
answers.tr: Hi, I'm Maria. I'm from Spain.

lessons.title: Read any word in this course
lessons.summary: Learn the small marks that show the vowels, so you can read every example by yourself.
lessons.topic: The vowel marks: fatḥa, kasra, ḍamma, sukūn, shadda, and the doubled endings

goal.tr: Thank you very much!
goal.note: by the end of the lesson, you can read this without the Latin letters

blocks.p: Arabic is written from right to left, and most letters join the letter after them. The letters mostly write **consonants**; the short vowels a, i and u are small marks above or below the letters.

blocks.means: a sound like a, i or u, made with the mouth open. The other sounds of speech, like b, k or s, are **consonants**.

blocks.p: Newspapers and street signs usually leave the marks out: readers know the words. Every example in this course has them, because they show exactly how a word is said, and some of them, as you'll see, are grammar.

**Long vowels** are written with letters: {{ا}} for ā, {{و}} for ū and {{ي}} for ī, as in {{بَابٌ|bābun}} “a door”, {{نُورٌ|nūrun}} “light” and {{كَبِيرٌ|kabīrun}} “big”. In the readings, a line over a vowel (ā, ī, ū) means it is long: hold it about twice as long.

**Doubled marks at the end** of a word ({{ـٌ}}, {{ـً}}, {{ـٍ}}) add an n: {{كِتَابٌ|kitābun}}, {{كِتَابًا|kitāban}}, {{كِتَابٍ|kitābin}}. They mean “a”, as in “a book”. Which one a word has depends on its job in the sentence; later lessons explain. That's the -an at the end of {{شُكْرًا}} and {{جَزِيلًا}}.

Two more signs: {{ء}} (hamza) is a short catch in the throat, like the break in “uh-oh”; it often sits on an alif, as in {{أَنَا|anā}} “I”. {{ة}}, a round t, ends many words (the lesson on masculine and feminine explains it). In the readings, ʾ is a hamza, ʿ is the letter {{ع}} (a sound made deep in the throat), and a dot under a letter (ḥ, ṣ, ḍ, ṭ, ẓ) marks a heavier sound than the plain one.

blocks.tip: Read the Arabic first, then check with the reading under it. Tap any example to hear it.

mistakes.why: The n of -un is never written as a letter: the doubled mark ({{ـٌ}}) already says it.
“Big” has a long ī, written with {{ي}}: kabīrun. Short and long vowels make different words, so hold the long ones.

practice.q: Which mark is the vowel i?
practice.why: The kasra, a small line **below** the letter, is i.

practice.q: What does the doubled mark at the end of {{كِتَابٌ}} add?
practice.why: {{ـٌ}} is said -un, and it means “a”: kitābun, a book.

practice.q: Which word has a long ā?
practice.why: The {{ا}} after the first letter makes a long ā: bābun.

practice.q: Read the words, then put them in order.
Read this word aloud, then check: {{مُدَرِّسٌ}}
practice.why: The shadda on {{ر}} says it twice: mu-dar-ri-sun.

practice.q: Your turn: read these aloud without looking at the Latin letters, then write how you would thank someone: {{شُكْرًا جَزِيلًا}}, {{مَرْحَبًا}}, {{أَنَا مِنْ هُنَا}}

lessons.title: Say what you want
lessons.summary: Ask for things, and say what you want to do: “I want to learn Arabic.”
lessons.topic: {{أُرِيدُ}} and what you want; {{أَنْ}} and the -a form of a verb (the subjunctive)

goal.tr: I want to learn Arabic.

dialog.t: لَا، شُكْرًا. وَأُرِيدُ أَنْ أَدْفَعَ الْآنَ.
dialog.r: lā, shukran. wa-urīdu an adfaʿa l-āna.
dialog.tr: No, thanks. And I'd like to pay now.

blocks.p: **Wanting a thing.** {{أُرِيدُ|urīdu}} “I want”, then what you want: {{أُرِيدُ قَهْوَةً.}} “I want a coffee.” The thing you want ends in -an here ({{قَهْوَةً|qahwatan}}, {{مَاءً|māʾan}} “water”, {{شَايًا|shāyan}} “tea”); a later lesson explains that ending, so for now just copy it.

blocks.means: a word for an action or a state: write, go, learn, want.

blocks.p: **Wanting to do something.** Put {{أَنْ|an}} “to” between {{أُرِيدُ}} and the second verb. Compare:

table: {{أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَتَعَلَّمَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ.|urīdu an ataʿallama l-ʿarabiyyata.}}

blocks.p: Two things change. {{أَنْ}} comes in, and the verb's last vowel turns from -u into -a: {{أَتَعَلَّمُ}} becomes {{أَنْ أَتَعَلَّمَ}}. And both verbs say who: {{أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ}} is, word for word, “I want that I go”.

blocks.means: a form of a verb used after certain little words, such as {{أَنْ}} “to”. In Arabic, the verb then ends in -a instead of -u.

ex.tr: I'd like a room for one night.
What do you want to eat?

blocks.tip: {{أُرِيدُ}} is polite enough in a shop or a café. Add {{مِنْ فَضْلِكَ|min faḍlika}} “please” (to a woman: {{مِنْ فَضْلِكِ|min faḍliki}}).

mistakes.why: Two verbs need {{أَنْ}} between them, and the second one ends in -a.
After {{أَنْ}}, the verb ends in -a, not -u.

practice.q: Which one means “I want to understand”?
practice.why: {{أَنْ}}, and the verb after it ends in -a.

practice.q: At the café: choose your replies.

lines.why: {{أُرِيدُ}} and what you want. ({{أَنَا شَايٌ}} would be “I am tea”!)

practice.q: How do you say “I want to learn Arabic”?
Your turn: what do you want to learn, and where do you want to go this year? Answer with {{أُرِيدُ أَنْ…}}

answers.tr: I want to go to Morocco.

answers.t: أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَتَكَلَّمَ مَعَ أَصْدِقَائِي بِالْعَرَبِيَّةِ.
answers.r: urīdu an atakallama maʿa aṣdiqāʾī bi-l-ʿarabiyyati.
answers.tr: I want to talk to my friends in Arabic.

lessons.title: Point at things and name them
lessons.summary: Ask “What's this?” and answer “This is a book”: and see why some words are “he” and others “she”.
lessons.topic: {{هَذَا}} and {{هَذِهِ}} “this (is)”; masculine and feminine, and the ending {{ة}}

goal.tr: What's this? It's a book.

blocks.p: {{هَذَا|hādhā}} is “this”, and, as in the first lesson, “is” isn't said: {{هَذَا قَلَمٌ}} is “this (is) a pen”. {{مَا|mā}} asks “what?”: {{مَا هَذَا؟}} “What's this?”
But the mother says {{هَذِهِ|hādhihi}} for the watch. That's because every Arabic noun is either masculine or feminine, and the word for “this” changes with it.

blocks.means: a word for a person, an animal, a place, a thing or an idea: teacher, cat, Cairo, book, love.
whether a word is **masculine** (like “he”) or **feminine** (like “she”). In Arabic every noun has one, even the words for things: a pen is masculine, a watch is feminine.

blocks.p: **The sign of the feminine**: most feminine nouns end in {{ة}}, a round t called tāʾ marbūṭa. It sounds -a at the end of a sentence and -at- before an ending: {{سَاعَةٌ|sāʿatun}} “a watch”. Many words for people make their feminine by adding it:

A few common feminine nouns have no {{ة}}; learn them as you meet them: {{أُمٌّ|ummun}} “mother”, {{بِنْتٌ|bintun}} “girl”, {{شَمْسٌ|shamsun}} “sun”, {{يَدٌ|yadun}} “hand”, and the names of most countries and cities.

ex.tr: This is a student, and this is a teacher.

blocks.tip: The long ā in {{هَذَا}} (hādhā) and {{هَذِهِ}} (hādhihi) isn't written as a letter, but it is said all the same.

mistakes.why: {{سَيَّارَةٌ}} is feminine (it ends in {{ة}}), so “this” is {{هَذِهِ}}.
A woman is a {{طَالِبَةٌ}}, with {{ة}}.

practice.why: It has no {{ة}}, but a mother is a woman: one of the feminine words to learn by heart.

practice.q: A friend points at things in your bag. Choose your replies.

lines.why: {{حَقِيبَةٌ}} “bag” is feminine: {{هَذِهِ}}. (And the word for “small” takes {{ة}} too: the next lessons show why.)

practice.q: A woman says “I'm a student”. What does she say?
Your turn: point at three things around you and name them with {{هَذَا…}} or {{هَذِهِ…}}.

lessons.title: Talk about “the” thing, not just “a” thing
lessons.summary: Say “a key” and “the key”, and ask where things are.
lessons.topic: {{الْـ}} “the”; the doubled mark means “a”; sun and moon letters

goal.tr: Where's the key?

blocks.p: Arabic's word for “the” is {{الْـ|al-}}. It is written joined to the front of the noun: {{مِفْتَاحٌ|miftāḥun}} is “a key”, {{الْمِفْتَاحُ|al-miftāḥu}} is “the key”.

There is no separate word for “a”: the doubled mark at the end (-un) already means it. With {{الْـ}}, the doubled mark goes and a single mark is left. So it's {{الْمِفْتَاحُ}}, never {{الْمِفْتَاحٌ}}: a word can't be “a” and “the” at once.

**Sun letters.** Before 14 of the letters, the l of {{الْـ}} isn't said: the next letter is doubled instead (it gets a shadda), though the l is still written. {{الشَّمْسُ}} “the sun” is said ash-shamsu. These are called sun letters, after {{شَمْسٌ}} “sun”; the others are moon letters, after {{قَمَرٌ}} “moon”, and with them the l is said: {{الْقَمَرُ|al-qamaru}}.

table: Sun letters: the l is not said
Moon letters: the l is said
{{ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن}}
{{ء ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م ه و ي}}

blocks.p: **After a vowel**, the a of {{الْـ}} isn't said either: {{أَيْنَ الْمِفْتَاحُ؟}} is ayna l-miftāḥu, and {{وَالْهَاتِفُ}} is wa-l-hātifu. The readings write it the way you hear it.

blocks.tip: Arabic also uses {{الْـ}} for things in general, where English uses nothing: “coffee is delicious” is {{الْقَهْوَةُ لَذِيذَةٌ}}, “the coffee is delicious”.

mistakes.why: A word with {{الْـ}} never has the doubled mark: that mark means “a”.
Before a sun letter the l is silent and has no mark of its own: say ash-shamsu.

practice.q: Choose the word that means “the car”.
practice.why: {{الْـ}} in front, and a single mark at the end.

practice.q: In which word is the l of {{الْـ}} **not** said?
Point at a book and say “This is a book.”
Your turn: ask where three things or places are, with {{أَيْنَ…؟}}

lessons.title: Describe people and things
lessons.summary: Say “a big house”, “the old city”, and “The food is delicious”.
lessons.topic: Adjectives: after the noun, matching it in gender, “a/the” and ending

goal.tr: The old city is very beautiful.

dialog.tr: The hotel is lovely, and the room is big.

blocks.means: a word that describes a noun: big, new, happy.

blocks.p: **Describing in a sentence**: as with “this is”, just put the two side by side: {{الْفُنْدُقُ جَمِيلٌ.}} “The hotel is lovely.” The noun has {{الْـ}}; the adjective hasn't. With a feminine noun, the adjective takes {{ة}} too: {{الْغُرْفَةُ كَبِيرَةٌ.}} “The room is big.”

**Describing inside a phrase** (“a big house”, “the old city”): the adjective comes **after** the noun and matches it in three ways: gender, “a” or “the”, and its ending. So “the old city” has {{الْـ}} twice: {{الْمَدِينَةُ الْقَدِيمَةُ|al-madīnatu l-qadīmatu}}.

That one {{الْـ}} makes all the difference: {{الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ}} is only a phrase, “the big house”; {{الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ}} is a sentence, “The house is big.” You can put both together: {{الْمَدِينَةُ الْقَدِيمَةُ جَمِيلَةٌ.}} “The old city is beautiful.”

blocks.tip: {{جِدًّا|jiddan}} “very” comes **after** the adjective: {{جَمِيلٌ جِدًّا}} “very beautiful”.

mistakes.why: The adjective comes after the noun.
{{سَيَّارَةٌ}} is feminine, so the adjective takes {{ة}} too.
With {{الْـ}} on both words it's a phrase, “the big house”. For a sentence, the adjective has no {{الْـ}}.

practice.why: Feminine ({{ة}}), and no {{الْـ}}: it's what you say about the car.
“The” on both words, and {{ة}} on both.
{{الْـ}} on the noun only: a sentence.

practice.q: How do you say “a beautiful city”?
Your turn: describe the place where you are now in two short sentences.

answers.tr: The room is small and nice.
The city is big and the weather is hot.

lessons.title: Ask questions
lessons.summary: Ask yes-or-no questions, and ask who, what, where, when, how and how much.
lessons.topic: {{هَلْ}} for yes-or-no questions; question words first

goal.t: عَفْوًا، أَيْنَ الْمَحَطَّةُ؟ هَلْ هِيَ بَعِيدَةٌ؟
goal.r: ʿafwan, ayna l-maḥaṭṭatu? hal hiya baʿīdatun?
goal.tr: Excuse me, where's the station? Is it far?

blocks.p: **Yes or no**: put {{هَلْ|hal}} in front of a sentence, and nothing else changes: {{هِيَ بَعِيدَةٌ.}} “It's far.” → {{هَلْ هِيَ بَعِيدَةٌ؟}} “Is it far?” In speech you can also just raise your voice at the end. The answers are {{نَعَمْ|naʿam}} “yes” and {{لَا|lā}} “no”.
Arabic's question mark faces the other way: {{؟}}. Before {{الْـ}}, {{هَلْ}} takes an i to join on: {{هَلِ الْمَطْعَمُ مَفْتُوحٌ؟|hali l-maṭʿamu maftūḥun?}} “Is the restaurant open?”
**Question words** come first, and the rest stays as it was: {{أَيْنَ}} + {{الْمَحَطَّةُ}} = “Where's the station?”

table: {{مَاذَا تُرِيدُ؟|mādhā turīdu?}} What do you want?
{{بِكَمْ هَذَا؟|bikam hādhā?}} How much is this?
{{لِمَاذَا أَنْتَ هُنَا؟|limādhā anta hunā?}} Why are you here?

ex.note: to a woman: ḥāluki; to a man: ḥāluka

blocks.tip: {{عَفْوًا|ʿafwan}} “excuse me” (it also means “you're welcome”) is the polite way to start a question to a stranger.

mistakes.why: {{هَلْ}} is only for yes-or-no questions; a question with a question word doesn't need it.
Before {{الْـ}}, {{هَلْ}} becomes {{هَلِ}}: hali l-maṭʿamu.

practice.q: How do you ask “Is the hotel near?”
practice.why: Yes or no: {{هَلْ}} in front of the sentence.

practice.q: In a shop. Choose your replies.

lines.why: A yes-or-no question: {{هَلْ}} and the sentence.

practice.q: Ask a woman where she's from.
Your turn: write three questions you'd ask someone you've just met.

lessons.title: Talk about other people: he, she, we, they
lessons.summary: Say who people are and what they do: “He's an engineer, and she's a doctor.”
lessons.topic: All the pronouns: {{هُوَ}}, {{هِيَ}}, {{نَحْنُ}}, {{أَنْتُمْ}}, {{هُمْ}}

goal.tr: He's an engineer, and she's a doctor.

dialog.tr: This is my brother. He's a student.
This is my sister. She's a teacher.
And where are you all from?

blocks.p: You know {{أَنَا}}, {{أَنْتَ}} and {{أَنْتِ}}. Here are all the words for people, the **pronouns**:

table: a man, or a masculine thing
a woman, or a feminine thing
any group with me in it
a group (of men, or men and women)

blocks.p: “It” is {{هُوَ}} or {{هِيَ}}, by the noun's gender: the station is feminine, so in the last lesson you asked {{هَلْ هِيَ بَعِيدَةٌ؟}} “Is it far?”
{{أَخِي|akhī}} “my brother” and {{أُخْتِي|ukhtī}} “my sister” end in -ī, “my”: a later lesson shows how it works with every noun.

Arabic also has words for a group of women only ({{هُنَّ|hunna}} “they”, {{أَنْتُنَّ|antunna}} “you”) and for exactly two people ({{هُمَا|humā}}, {{أَنْتُمَا|antumā}}). You'll hear them less; a later lesson comes back to the two.

blocks.tip: Plurals for people often end in -ūna ({{مَشْغُولُونَ}} “busy”), but many change shape ({{أَصْدِقَاءُ}} “friends”). A later lesson explains; for now learn them as you meet them.

mistakes.why: A woman: the word takes {{ة}}.
“We” needs a plural word: {{أَصْدِقَاءُ}} “friends”.

practice.q: “The car? It's new.” Which word is “it”: {{السَّيَّارَةُ؟ ___ جَدِيدَةٌ.}}
Introduce your friend Karim: “This is Karim. He's an engineer.”
Your turn: tell someone about two people you know: who they are and what they do.

answers.tr: This is my friend. He's a teacher.
This is my sister. She's a student.

lessons.title: Say where things and people are
lessons.summary: “The keys are on the table”, “I'm at work”, “from the airport to the hotel”: the little words for place.
lessons.topic: Prepositions ({{فِي}}, {{عَلَى}}, {{مِنْ}}, {{إِلَى}}…) and the -i ending after them

goal.tr: The key is on the table.

dialog.tr: I'm in the café, near the station.
She's on her way from the airport.

blocks.means: a small word that links a noun to the rest of the sentence, often to say where or when: in, on, from, to, with.

table: {{أَمَامَ الْفُنْدُقِ|amāma l-funduqi}} in front of the hotel

blocks.p: **The -i ending.** After a preposition, the noun ends in -i: {{الطَّاوِلَةُ|aṭ-ṭāwilatu}} becomes {{عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ|ʿalā ṭ-ṭāwilati}}. Without “the”, -un becomes -in: {{صَدِيقٌ}}, but {{مَعَ صَدِيقٍ|maʿa ṣadīqin}}.

blocks.means: the vowel at the end of an Arabic noun, which changes with the noun's job in the sentence: -u, -a or -i (-un, -an, -in when it means “a”). After a preposition it is always -i.

blocks.p: Before {{الْـ}}, {{مِنْ}} becomes {{مِنَ|mina}}, as {{هَلْ}} became {{هَلِ}}: two consonants can't meet. Three prepositions are written joined to the next word: {{بِـ|bi-}} “by, with”, {{لِـ|li-}} “for” and {{كَـ|ka-}} “like”: {{بِالسَّيَّارَةِ|bi-s-sayyārati}} “by car”, {{لِلْمُعَلِّمِ|lil-muʿallimi}} “for the teacher” ({{لِـ}} drops the alif of {{الْـ}}).

ex.tr: The restaurant is in front of the hotel.
The road to the airport is long.
This present is for the teacher.

blocks.tip: Names of most countries and cities don't take -in: after a preposition they end in -a. {{أَنَا مِنْ مِصْرَ.|anā min miṣra.}} “I'm from Egypt.”

mistakes.why: After a preposition, the noun ends in -i.
Before {{الْـ}}, {{مِنْ}} becomes {{مِنَ}}: mina l-maṭāri.

practice.tr: The key is on the table.

practice.q: A friend calls. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: Is the restaurant near the house?

practice.q: How do you say “I'm from Egypt”?
practice.why: Country names end in -a after a preposition: {{مِصْرَ}}.

practice.q: Your turn: say where you are now, and where three things around you are.

answers.tr: The phone is on the table.
The cat is under the bed.

lessons.title: Say what there is: “There's a café near here”
lessons.summary: Say what a place has, and ask “Is there a pharmacy here?”
lessons.topic: “There is”: the place first; {{هُنَاكَ}} and {{يُوجَدُ}}

goal.tr: Is there a restaurant nearby?

dialog.tr: Excuse me, is there a restaurant nearby?

dialog.t: نَعَمْ، هُنَاكَ مَطْعَمٌ جَمِيلٌ أَمَامَ الْفُنْدُقِ.
dialog.r: naʿam, hunāka maṭʿamun jamīlun amāma l-funduqi.
dialog.tr: Yes, there's a nice restaurant in front of the hotel.
And is there internet in the room?

blocks.p: To say that something is somewhere, start with the place, then the thing, without “the”: {{فِي الْغُرْفَةِ سَرِيرٌ.|fī l-ghurfati sarīrun.}} “There's a bed in the room.” (word for word: in the room, a bed). An Arabic sentence doesn't start with a noun that means “a…”, so the place comes first.

You can also start with {{هُنَاكَ|hunāka}} “there”: {{هُنَاكَ مُشْكِلَةٌ.|hunāka mushkilatun.}} “There's a problem.” Polite and written Arabic often use {{يُوجَدُ|yūjadu}} “there is” (word for word: is found).
**There isn't:** {{لَا يُوجَدُ|lā yūjadu}}: {{لَا يُوجَدُ وَقْتٌ.|lā yūjadu waqtun.}} “There's no time.” **Is there…?:** {{هَلْ يُوجَدُ…؟}} or {{هَلْ هُنَاكَ…؟}}

ex.tr: There's a café near the station.
There's a book on the table.

blocks.tip: Compare {{الْكِتَابُ عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ.}} “The book is on the table.” (a book you both know) and {{عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ كِتَابٌ.}} “There's a book on the table.” (some book).

mistakes.tr: There's a book on the table.
mistakes.why: Don't start with a noun meaning “a…”: put the place first.
“There is” brings in something new: no {{الْـ}}.

practice.q: “There's a café near the station” is…
practice.why: Start with {{هُنَاكَ}}, and the café without “the”.

practice.q: Your turn: say what there is in your street or town, and ask about something you need.

answers.tr: There's a small café in the street.

lessons.title: Say whose it is: my, your, his
lessons.summary: Say “my name”, “your bag”, “her phone”: Arabic adds a short ending to the noun.
lessons.topic: The possessive endings ({{ـِي}}, {{ـكَ}}, {{ـكِ}}, {{ـهُ}}, {{ـهَا}}…)

goal.tr: What's your name? My name is Karim.

dialog.tr: My passport is here, in my bag.

blocks.p: Arabic has no separate words for “my”, “your”, “his”. A short ending is joined to the noun instead, and the noun drops {{الْـ}} and its doubled mark: the ending already says whose it is.

blocks.means: a short ending joined to a noun to say whose it is, like “my” or “your” in English: {{كِتَابِي}} “my book”.

blocks.p: **The round t opens up**: {{ة}} becomes an ordinary {{ت}} before an ending, and is said: {{حَقِيبَةٌ|ḥaqībatun}} “a bag”, {{حَقِيبَتِي|ḥaqībatī}} “my bag”.

The case ending stays between the noun and the ending: {{بَيْتُهُ|baytuhu}} “his house”, but {{فِي بَيْتِهِ|fī baytihi}} “in his house” (-i after {{فِي}}, and -hu becomes -hi after an i). Only “my” swallows it: {{فِي بَيْتِي|fī baytī}}.

A noun with an ending counts as “the”: so {{سَيَّارَتِي جَدِيدَةٌ.}} is a sentence, “My car is new”, and “my new car” is {{سَيَّارَتِي الْجَدِيدَةُ|sayyāratī l-jadīdatu}}, with {{الْـ}} on the adjective.

blocks.tip: {{اسْمٌ}} “name” starts with a vowel that is only said at the start of a sentence: {{اسْمِي سَارَةُ|ismī sāratu}}, but {{مَا اسْمُكَ؟|mā smuka?}}.

mistakes.why: A noun with an ending never has {{الْـ}} too.
{{ة}} becomes {{ت}} before an ending.

practice.tr: My passport is in my bag.

practice.q: Your turn: tell someone your name, and one thing about your home or your family.

answers.tr: My name is John. My house is small.
My name is Lina. My mother is a teacher.

lessons.title: Talk about what you have
lessons.summary: Say “I have a question”, “Do you have time?”, “She has two brothers”: Arabic says “at me”, “for me”, “with me”.
lessons.topic: No verb “to have”: {{عِنْدِي}}, {{لِي}}, {{مَعِي}}; endings on prepositions

goal.tr: I have a question.

dialog.tr: Excuse me, I have a question.
Do you have time after the lesson?
Unfortunately, I don't have time today.

blocks.p: To say “I have”, Arabic says “at me (there is)…”: {{عِنْدِي|ʿindī}}, made of {{عِنْدَ}} “at” and the ending “my”. Then what you have: {{عِنْدِي سَيَّارَةٌ.|ʿindī sayyāratun.}} “I have a car.” The thing you have keeps -un: in Arabic it's the subject of the sentence.

blocks.means: who or what does the action, or what the sentence is about. In “The train arrives”, the subject is “the train”; in {{عِنْدِي سَيَّارَةٌ}} “I have a car”, it is the car.

blocks.p: Two other little words do the same job. {{لِـ}} “for” is used for family and lasting things: {{لِي أَخٌ.|lī akhun.}} “I have a brother.” (with the other endings it is {{لَـ}}: {{لَكَ}}, {{لَهُ}}, {{لَهَا}}). And {{مَعَ}} “with” means you have it on you, now: {{مَعِي مَالٌ.|maʿī mālun.}} “I have money on me.”

**Not having:** {{لَيْسَ|laysa}} in front: {{لَيْسَ عِنْدِي وَقْتٌ.}} “I don't have time.” (A later lesson explains {{لَيْسَ}}.) The same endings go on every preposition: {{مِنْهُ}} “from him”, {{مَعَهَا}} “with her”, {{عَلَيْهِ}} “on it”, {{فِيهِ}} “in it”.

ex.tr: He has a son and a daughter.
Have you got a pen on you?
ex.note: to a man; a question just by the voice

blocks.tip: {{عِنْدِي}} is the everyday word: when in doubt, use it.

mistakes.why: The thing you have is the subject, so it keeps -un.
With an ending, {{لِـ}} becomes {{لَـ}}: lahu. Only “my” is {{لِي}}.

practice.q: Which fits best for “I've got money on me (right now)”?
practice.why: {{مَعَ}} “with” is for what you have on you.

practice.q: At the hotel desk. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: Hello! Do you have a booking?

practice.q: Ask a man: “Do you have a pen?”
Your turn: say two things you have and one you don't have.

lessons.title: Join two nouns: “the teacher's book”, “a cup of coffee”
lessons.summary: Put two nouns side by side to say whose something is, or what kind it is.
lessons.topic: The iḍāfa: two nouns together

goal.tr: A cup of coffee, please.

dialog.tr: Excuse me, where's the train station?
Past the gate of the old city.
And is there a tourist office?
Yes, in front of the station.

blocks.p: To say “the teacher's book” or “the door of the house”, Arabic puts the two nouns side by side: first the thing, then whose it is: {{كِتَابُ الْمُعَلِّمِ|kitābu l-muʿallimi}}, word for word “book the-teacher”.

blocks.means: two (or more) nouns side by side, the second saying whose the first is or what kind it is: {{بَابُ الْبَيْتِ}} “the door of the house”. The word means “adding”.

blocks.p: **Three rules.** 1) The first noun never has {{الْـ}} or the doubled mark, even though it means “the”: {{بَابُ|bābu}}. 2) The second noun ends in -i (or -in), as after a preposition: {{الْبَيْتِ|al-bayti}}. 3) A {{ة}} on the first noun is said with its t: {{مَحَطَّةُ الْقِطَارِ|maḥaṭṭatu l-qiṭāri}}.

If the second noun has “the” (or an ending like “my”), the pair means “the…”: {{بَابُ الْبَيْتِ}} “the door of the house”, {{سَيَّارَةُ أَبِي|sayyāratu abī}} “my father's car”. If not, it means “a…” or says what kind: {{فِنْجَانُ قَهْوَةٍ}} “a cup of coffee”, {{مَكْتَبُ سِيَاحَةٍ}} “a tourist office”.
An adjective comes after the whole pair, matching the noun it describes: {{سَيَّارَةُ أَبِي الْجَدِيدَةُ|sayyāratu abī l-jadīdatu}} “my father's new car”.

ex.tr: The door of the house is open.

blocks.tip: Chains work too: {{بَابُ بَيْتِ الْمُدِيرِ|bābu bayti l-mudīri}} “the door of the manager's house”. Only the last noun can have {{الْـ}}.

mistakes.why: The first noun never takes {{الْـ}} (or the doubled mark).
The second noun ends in -i.

practice.why: The second noun of the pair ends in -i.
First noun bare, second with {{الْـ}} and -i.
The adjective comes after the whole pair.

practice.tr: The door of the house is open.

practice.q: Order in a café: “A cup of coffee, please” (to a man).
Your turn: ask where three places in a town are, each with two nouns together.

lessons.title: Say what something isn't
lessons.summary: Say “I'm not tired”, “The shop isn't open”, “We're not from here”.
lessons.topic: {{لَيْسَ}} “is not”, its forms, and the -a ending after it

goal.tr: I'm not tired, I'm just hungry!

dialog.tr: And the hospital? Is it far?

blocks.p: Sentences without a verb (“The pharmacy is open”) are made negative with {{لَيْسَ|laysa}} “is not”. Unlike “is”, which isn't said, “is not” is a real word, and it changes with the person:

**The -a ending.** What you say about the subject now ends in -a, or -an without “the”, written with an extra alif ({{ـًا}}): {{أَنَا مُتْعَبٌ.}} “I'm tired.” → {{لَسْتُ مُتْعَبًا.|lastu mutʿaban.}} “I'm not tired.” Words ending in {{ة}} add no alif: {{لَيْسَتْ مَفْتُوحَةً}}.

ex.note: a man speaking; a woman: {{لَسْتُ مُتْعَبَةً|lastu mutʿabatan}}

blocks.tip: Only a noun or an adjective after {{لَيْسَ}} takes -a. A place doesn't change ({{هِيَ لَيْسَتْ فِي الْبَيْتِ}} “She isn't at home”), and with {{عِنْدِي}} the thing keeps -un ({{لَيْسَ عِنْدِي وَقْتٌ}}).

mistakes.why: {{لَا}} is for verbs; a sentence without a verb takes {{لَيْسَ}}.
After {{لَيْسَ}}, the adjective ends in -an.

practice.why: {{لَسْتُ}} for “I am not”, and -an on the adjective.

practice.q: Your turn: correct someone who is wrong about you: “I'm not…, I'm…”

answers.tr: I'm not a student, I'm a teacher.

answers.t: لَسْتُ مِنْ مِصْرَ، أَنَا مِنَ الْمَغْرِبِ.
answers.r: lastu min miṣra, anā mina l-maghribi.
answers.tr: I'm not from Egypt, I'm from Morocco.

lessons.title: Shop: this one, that one, how much?
lessons.summary: Point at what you want in a shop, ask the price, and say “this bag” and “that one”.
lessons.topic: {{هَذَا}}, {{هَذِهِ}}, {{ذَلِكَ}}, {{تِلْكَ}}: “this bag” vs “this is a bag”

goal.tr: How much is this bag?

blocks.p: **“This bag” or “This is a bag”?** A pointing word before a noun **with** {{الْـ}} makes a phrase: {{هَذِهِ الْحَقِيبَةُ|hādhihi l-ḥaqībatu}} “this bag”. Before a noun **without** {{الْـ}}, it makes a sentence: {{هَذِهِ حَقِيبَةٌ.}} “This is a bag.” To say “This is **the** bag”, add {{هِيَ}} or {{هُوَ}}: {{هَذِهِ هِيَ الْحَقِيبَةُ.}}
{{ذَلِكَ}} and {{تِلْكَ}} point at things further away. For things (not people) in the plural, Arabic says {{هَذِهِ}} and {{تِلْكَ}}: {{هَذِهِ الْكُتُبُ}} “these books” (a later lesson explains why).

blocks.tip: Prices: just say the number and the money, or {{بِـ}} + the price: {{بِعَشَرَةِ دَرَاهِمَ}} “for ten dirhams”. The numbers come in a later lesson; until then, point and listen.

mistakes.why: To say “this book is new”, the book needs {{الْـ}}. Without it: “This is a new book.”
{{رَجُلٌ}} “man” is masculine.

practice.why: Feminine, and a phrase: {{الْـ}} on the noun.
No {{الْـ}} on the noun: a sentence.

practice.q: At the market. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: Go ahead, what would you like?

lines.why: “That bag” is a phrase: {{الْـ}} on the noun.

practice.q: Ask the price of this bag.
Your turn: in a shop, ask for one thing near you and one further away, and ask a price.

answers.tr: I'd like this shirt and that bag.

lessons.title: Say what you do: “I live…, I work…, I study…”
lessons.summary: Talk about your life: where you live, where you work or study, how you get there.
lessons.topic: The present tense: I, you, he, she (a letter in front says who)

goal.t: أَسْكُنُ فِي الْقَاهِرَةِ، وَأَعْمَلُ فِي بَنْكٍ.
goal.r: askunu fī l-qāhirati, wa-aʿmalu fī bankin.
goal.tr: I live in Cairo, and I work in a bank.

dialog.tr: No, I work in a hospital. And you?

blocks.means: the form of a verb that shows when something happens: now (the present), before (the past) or later (the future).

blocks.p: An Arabic verb in the present is its root with a letter in front that says **who** does it, and -u at the end. From {{س ك ن}} “living (somewhere)”:

The Arabic present is also English's “-ing”: {{أَعْمَلُ}} is “I work” and “I'm working”. And since the verb already says who, the pronoun is usually left out: {{أَسْكُنُ فِي الْقَاهِرَةِ}}. Lina's {{أَنَا أَدْرُسُ}} stresses “me”: “*I* study medicine”.

**Learning verbs.** The vowel after the second root letter changes from verb to verb: {{يَسْكُنُ|yaskunu}} “lives”, {{يَعْمَلُ|yaʿmalu}} “works”, {{يَجْلِسُ|yajlisu}} “sits”. Dictionaries give each verb as “he did, he does”: {{سَكَنَ يَسْكُنُ}}. Learn both.

ex.tr: I go to work by bus.

ex.note: to a man; {{مَاذَا}} is “what” before a verb

blocks.tip: “You” (to a man) and “she” look the same in the present: {{تَسْكُنُ}}. Who it is comes from the conversation.

mistakes.why: The letter in front must match the person: {{أَ}} for “I”.
Talking to a woman, the verb ends in -īna.

practice.why: The ending -īna is for one woman.

practice.q: Someone asks about you. Choose your replies.
Ask a woman: “Where do you live?”
Your turn: say where you live, and where you work or study.

answers.t: أَسْكُنُ فِي لَنْدَنَ، وَأَعْمَلُ فِي مَكْتَبٍ.
answers.r: askunu fī landana, wa-aʿmalu fī maktabin.
answers.tr: I live in London, and I work in an office.

answers.t: أَسْكُنُ قُرْبَ الْبَحْرِ، وَأَدْرُسُ فِي الْجَامِعَةِ.
answers.r: askunu qurba l-baḥri, wa-adrusu fī l-jāmiʿati.
answers.tr: I live near the sea, and I study at the university.

lessons.title: Say what others do: we, you all, they
lessons.summary: Talk about your family and friends: “We live near the sea”, “They're playing in the garden”.
lessons.topic: The present tense: we, you (group), they; the whole pattern

goal.t: نَسْكُنُ قُرْبَ الْبَحْرِ، وَالْأَوْلَادُ يَلْعَبُونَ هُنَاكَ.
goal.r: naskunu qurba l-baḥri, wa-l-awlādu yalʿabūna hunāka.
goal.tr: We live near the sea, and the children play there.

dialog.tr: And when are you all coming back home?
We're coming back in the evening.

blocks.p: So the whole present has one shape: a letter in front ({{أَ}} I, {{تَ}} you and she, {{يَ}} he and they, {{نَ}} we) and an ending for some persons (-īna for one woman, -ūna for a group). Three verbs in full:
A group of women only has forms of its own ({{يَكْتُبْنَ|yaktubna}} “they write”), and so do two people; you'll see them in writing more than you hear them.

ex.tr: We go to the market on Fridays.

blocks.tip: Listen for the -ūna: it tells “they write” ({{يَكْتُبُونَ}}) from “he writes” ({{يَكْتُبُ}}).

mistakes.why: After “they”, the verb takes -ūna.
“We” is {{نَ}} in front: naskunu.

practice.tr: We're coming back in the evening.

practice.why: {{يَ}} in front and -ūna at the end: “they”.

practice.q: Ask a group: “Where do you live?”
practice.why: {{تَ}} in front and -ūna for a group of you.

practice.q: Your turn: say where your family or friends live and what they do.

answers.tr: My family live in a small village.
We work at the same company.

lessons.title: Say what you like, eat and drink
lessons.summary: “I love Arabic food”, “I drink tea every morning”, “She's reading a book”: the thing you act on.
lessons.topic: The object of a verb and its -a ending

goal.t: أُحِبُّ الطَّعَامَ الْعَرَبِيَّ، وَأَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ كُلَّ صَبَاحٍ.
goal.r: uḥibbu ṭ-ṭaʿāma l-ʿarabiyya, wa-ashrabu sh-shāya kulla ṣabāḥin.
goal.tr: I love Arabic food, and I drink tea every morning.

dialog.tr: Yes, I really like Arabic coffee.
Here you are, and here's some cake.
Thanks! I'll have just one piece.

blocks.means: the person or thing a verb acts on. In “I love coffee”, the object is “coffee”.

blocks.p: The object of a verb ends in **-a**: {{الْقَهْوَةُ|al-qahwatu}} becomes {{أُحِبُّ الْقَهْوَةَ.|uḥibbu l-qahwata.}} “I like coffee.” That is the -a you have been copying since {{أُرِيدُ قَهْوَةً}}.

Without “the”, the ending is **-an**, written with an extra alif: {{كِتَابٌ}} → {{أَقْرَأُ كِتَابًا.|aqraʾu kitāban.}} “I'm reading a book.” Words in {{ة}} add no alif: {{أَكْتُبُ رِسَالَةً.|aktubu risālatan.}} “I'm writing a letter.” An adjective takes the same ending as its noun: {{الطَّعَامَ الْعَرَبِيَّ}}.
So you now know all three case endings: -u for the subject, -a for the object, -i after a preposition. A lesson soon puts them side by side.

ex.tr: My father buys bread every day.

blocks.tip: Some verbs have u- in front instead of a-: {{أُرِيدُ|urīdu}} “I want”, {{أُحِبُّ|uḥibbu}} “I love”, {{تُحِبُّ|tuḥibbu}} “you love”. A later lesson on verb families explains why; for now, learn them as they are.

mistakes.why: The object ends in -a.
Without “the”, the object ends in -an, written {{ـًا}}.

practice.q: Which word is the object in {{نُحِبُّ الطَّعَامَ الْعَرَبِيَّ}}?
practice.why: {{الطَّعَامَ}} is what we love, and it ends in -a.

practice.q: A friend invites you to eat. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: What do you like? Fish or meat?
And will you have some juice?

practice.q: Ask a man: “Do you know the way?”
Your turn: say what you like to eat and drink, and what you have every morning.

lessons.title: Say what you don't do
lessons.summary: “I don't understand”, “He doesn't drink coffee”, “We don't work on Saturdays”.
lessons.topic: {{لَا}} before a verb in the present

goal.tr: Sorry, I don't understand.

dialog.t: إِلَى الْفُنْدُقِ، لَكِنْ لَا أَعْرِفُ الْعُنْوَانَ.
dialog.r: ilā l-funduqi, lākin lā aʿrifu l-ʿunwāna.
dialog.tr: To the hotel, but I don't know the address.
The Nile Hotel. Do you know it?

blocks.p: To make a verb in the present negative, put {{لَا|lā}} in front of it. Nothing else changes: {{أَعْرِفُ|aʿrifu}} “I know” → {{لَا أَعْرِفُ.|lā aʿrifu.}} “I don't know.”

{{لَا}} is only for verbs. A sentence without a verb takes {{لَيْسَ}}, which you met earlier: {{لَسْتُ مُتْعَبًا}} “I'm not tired”, but {{لَا أَنَامُ}} “I don't sleep”. On its own, {{لَا}} is the answer “no”.

blocks.tip: {{لَا أَفْهَمُ}} and {{مِنْ فَضْلِكَ، بِبُطْءٍ|min faḍlika, bi-buṭʾin}} “slowly, please” are two of the most useful sentences of your first weeks.

mistakes.why: With a verb, use {{لَا}}; {{لَيْسَ}} is for sentences without a verb.
{{لَا}} comes before the verb.

practice.q: Tell someone politely that you don't understand, and ask them to speak slowly.
Your turn: say two things you don't do, and one thing you do instead.

answers.tr: I don't drink coffee, I drink tea.

lessons.title: Say “I know him”, “Help me”, “I love you”
lessons.summary: Put “me, you, him, her, us, them” after a verb.
lessons.topic: Object endings on verbs ({{ـنِي}}, {{ـكَ}}, {{ـهُ}}, {{ـهَا}}…)

goal.tr: Do you understand me? Yes, I understand you.

dialog.tr: Yes, I know him well. He's my neighbour.

blocks.p: “Him”, “her”, “you” after a verb are the endings you know from “my”, “your”, “his”, joined to the verb: {{أَعْرِفُهُ.|aʿrifuhu.}} “I know him.”, {{لَا أَعْرِفُهَا.}} “I don't know her.”

Only “me” is different: on a verb it is {{ـنِي|-nī}}, not {{ـِي}}: {{أَخِي يُسَاعِدُنِي.|akhī yusāʿidunī.}} “My brother helps me.” And “it” is {{ـهُ}} or {{ـهَا}} by the noun's gender: {{السَّيَّارَةُ جَمِيلَةٌ، أُرِيدُهَا.}} “The car is beautiful, I want it.”

ex.tr: This food is delicious, I love it.

blocks.tip: The verb keeps its -u before the ending: {{أَعْرِفُ}} + {{ـهُ}} = {{أَعْرِفُهُ|aʿrifuhu}}.

mistakes.why: On a verb, “me” is {{ـنِي}}.
{{هُوَ}} is only a subject; as an object, “him” is the ending {{ـهُ}}.

practice.tr: His wife? No, I don't know her.

practice.why: {{لَا}} before the verb, and “them” as the ending -hum.

practice.tr: We're waiting for you here. (to a man)

practice.q: Your turn: say who you know well, and something you love (with “it”).

answers.tr: This city is beautiful, I love it.

lessons.title: Read the news: the verb first
lessons.summary: Arabic often starts with the verb: “Arrives the train…”. And then the verb stays singular, even for “the students”.
lessons.topic: Word order: verb first or subject first, and how the verb agrees

goal.tr: The train arrives in the evening.

blocks.p: With a noun as the subject, Arabic can put the verb first. That is usual in writing and the news: {{يَصِلُ الْقِطَارُ فِي الْمَسَاءِ.}} “The train arrives in the evening.” (word for word: arrives the train in the evening). The subject first is also correct, and common in speech: {{الْقِطَارُ يَصِلُ فِي الْمَسَاءِ.}}
**The rule to remember:** when the verb comes **first**, it stays singular, even with a plural subject; it only matches the gender. When the subject comes first, the verb matches it completely.

table: {{يَذْهَبُ الطُّلَّابُ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ.|yadhhabu ṭ-ṭullābu ilā l-madrasati.}}
{{الطُّلَّابُ يَذْهَبُونَ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ.|aṭ-ṭullābu yadhhabūna ilā l-madrasati.}}

blocks.p: With a feminine subject, the verb takes {{تَ}} in front wherever it stands: {{تَعْمَلُ أُمِّي فِي مَدْرَسَةٍ.|taʿmalu ummī fī madrasatin.}} “My mother works at a school.”

ex.tr: The travellers are waiting at the airport.
The travellers are waiting at the airport.
My mother works at a school.

blocks.tip: Both orders are correct. You'll read the verb-first order in newspapers; in conversation, the subject first is just as natural.

mistakes.why: A verb before its subject stays singular.

mistakes.tr: My mother works at a school.
mistakes.why: A feminine subject: the verb takes {{تَ}} in front.

practice.tr: The travellers are waiting at the airport.

practice.why: Subject first: the verb matches it fully.

practice.tr: The train arrives in the evening.

practice.q: Say “People love this restaurant”, verb first.
Your turn: write a short “news” sentence about someone in your family, verb first.

answers.tr: My brother works at a big company.

lessons.title: See who does what: the three endings
lessons.summary: Put together the endings -u, -a and -i, and learn when speakers leave them out.
lessons.topic: The three case endings side by side; dropping endings at a pause

goal.tr: The girl loves the cat.
goal.note: the endings tell you who loves whom

blocks.p: You have now met all three case endings. Side by side:

table: the subject, and what you say about it
after a preposition; the second noun of an iḍāfa

blocks.p: One sentence with all three: {{يَقْرَأُ الطَّالِبُ الْكِتَابَ فِي الْمَكْتَبَةِ.|yaqraʾu ṭ-ṭālibu l-kitāba fī l-maktabati.}} “The student is reading the book in the library.” The student does it (-u), the book is what is read (-a), the library comes after {{فِي}} (-i). The endings let Arabic say who did what, whatever the order.
Their Arabic names are marfūʿ (-u), manṣūb (-a) and majrūr (-i); English grammars call them nominative, accusative and genitive.

**In speech, the last ending is dropped.** At the end of a sentence, or before a pause, speakers don't say the final short vowel, or -un and -in: {{الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ.}} is said al-baytu kabīr, and {{ة}} is said -a: {{مَدِينَةٌ}} madīna. In relaxed talk many people drop endings inside the sentence too; news readers and teachers say them.

A few kinds of nouns don't show all three: names and some plurals never take -un, and use -a where you'd expect -i ({{مِنْ مِصْرَ}}, {{أَصْدِقَاءُ}}); nouns ending in a long ā never show their ending ({{مُسْتَشْفًى}}, {{الْمَقْهَى}}). Learn them as you meet them.

ex.tr: The student is reading the book in the library.
My father drinks tea in the morning.
I want a room in a quiet hotel.

ex.note: said at a pause: ṣadīqī muhandis

blocks.tip: Don't let the endings slow you down when you speak. Say the words without them at a pause, as everyone does; when you read, use them to see who does what.

mistakes.tr: The student is reading the book.
mistakes.why: The one reading is the subject (-u); the thing read is the object (-a).
After a preposition: -in.

practice.q: In {{تُحِبُّ الْبِنْتُ الْقِطَّةَ}}, who loves whom?
practice.why: {{الْبِنْتُ}} has -u: the subject; {{الْقِطَّةَ}} has -a: the object.

practice.tr: I want a room in a quiet hotel.

practice.q: Which ending does the noun after {{لَيْسَ}} take?

practice.tr: My father drinks tea in the morning.

practice.q: Say “My friend is an engineer”, as you'd say it at the end of a sentence.
practice.why: At a pause the final -un is dropped: muhandis.

practice.q: Your turn: write one sentence with a subject, an object and a place (like the student reading in the library).

answers.tr: My mother drinks coffee in the kitchen.
The children read stories in the room.
